title: Dyeing with brazilwood
subtitle: Pink to red tones on alum-mordanted wool from this historic trade dye
excerpt: Brazilwood chips give pink to coral-red tones on alum-mordanted wool. The dye is extracted from the heartwood of Caesalpinia species and was among the most widely traded dyestuffs from the 15th century onward. It is available as chips or powder from specialist dye suppliers.
sourceNotes: Hummel, The Dyeing of Textile Fabrics (1885), Internet Archive. Hummel covers brazilwood dyeing extensively as a well-established historical dye. Pellew, Dyes and Dyeing (1913), Internet Archive, describes the mordant procedure with alum and the colour shift with iron.

attrs.title: Mordant safety
attrs.body: Dye-pot work outdoors. Dedicated pot and utensils only. Gloves and apron. Alum bath can compost. Iron bath via foul drain only.

attrs.title: Dye source
attrs.body: Brazilwood is available as chips or powder from specialist natural dye suppliers. It is a traded historical dye; it does not correspond to a Garden tutorial entry.

items.name: Brazilwood chips
items.qty: 50 to 100% of dry fibre weight for a medium pink-red

items.name: Vinegar or baking soda for pH adjustment

content.text: Soak the brazilwood chips in cold water overnight to begin extracting the dye. Mordant the wool in a standard alum bath at 15% weight-of-fibre: dissolve alum in hot water, add to a pot of warm water, enter the pre-wetted wool at 40°C, raise to 80°C over 30 minutes, hold for 45 minutes, cool and remove.

Simmer the soaked chips in fresh water at 80°C for 60 minutes. Strain and return the dye liquor to the pot. The liquor will be a deep red-brown. Add a small amount of vinegar at this point (one tablespoon per litre) to shift the dye-bath slightly acid and promote pinker-red tones.

Enter the mordanted fibre into the dye-bath at 40°C. Raise slowly to 80°C and hold for 60 minutes, turning regularly. Do not go above 85°C: high temperatures shift the colour toward orange-brown and reduce the pinker tones. Let the bath cool with the fibre in it, then rinse in warm water and dry in shade away from direct light.

Adding half a teaspoon of baking soda to the dye-bath after entering the fibre shifts the colour from pink-red toward violet-red: the alkali changes the dye's spectral absorption. This shift is reversible: a subsequent vinegar rinse returns the colour toward pink. An iron after-bath shifts the colour toward dark coral or maroon; use iron in small amounts and test on a small sample before committing the full skein.

items.problem: The colour shifted from pink to brownish-orange during dyeing
items.cause: The dye-bath temperature was too high, or the bath was too alkaline
items.fix: Keep the bath below 85°C and add a small amount of vinegar to ensure the bath stays slightly acid. High-temperature and alkaline conditions both push brazilwood toward orange-brown.

items.problem: The colour faded within a few weeks of finishing
items.cause: Brazilwood is not highly light-fast; exposure to daylight quickly reduces the pink-red tones
items.fix: Keep brazilwood-dyed items out of direct light. For an item that will be used or displayed in light, consider overdyeing with a more light-fast dye (such as weld) to produce an orange-red that holds its colour better.
